parts.context: The coordinator and the director of a seniors’ centre are discussing a problem with their volunteer driving program.

lines: Tariq, have you got a minute? I’ve just had a call from our insurance broker, and I’m afraid it affects the drive program.

The company that provides our excess liability coverage, the policy that sits on top of the volunteers’ own car insurance, is pulling out of the non-profit market altogether. They’re not renewing anyone. Our policy ends on the thirtieth.
The thirtieth of this month? That’s barely three weeks away.

Twenty-two days. And you know what the board said when we set the program up: no excess coverage, no volunteer drivers. They were very firm about it, and frankly I agree with them. If a volunteer caused a serious accident with a client in the car, their personal policy could run out very quickly.
How many clients are we talking about?

Thirty-eight people use it regularly. Most of it is medical appointments: dialysis, cancer treatment, eye injections. About sixty rides a month. For some of them, it’s the only way they get to the hospital at all.
And the drivers? I’m worried we’ll lose them if the program goes on hold, even briefly.
So am I. Fourteen active volunteers, and half of them are retirees who told me they’d happily find another cause if we leave them sitting at home. Recruiting new drivers took us two years.
Right. Well, the budget line for insurance is thirty-two hundred a year. Did the broker give you any alternatives?
She’s getting quotes. She said not to expect anything close to what we were paying.

qs.q: Why will the drive program lose its insurance coverage?
o: The centre missed the deadline to renew the policy.
The insurer is leaving that market completely.
A volunteer was involved in a serious accident.
The board decided the policy was too expensive.
qs.ev: is pulling out of the non-profit market altogether
qs.x: The insurer is “pulling out of the non-profit market altogether” and renewing no one. The serious accident is only a hypothetical risk, and the board’s rule concerns having coverage, not its cost.

qs.q: What is Agnes’s view of the board’s rule about volunteer drivers?
o: She thinks it is too strict in an emergency.
She plans to ask the board to suspend it.
She believes most volunteers are unaware of it.
She supports it despite the difficulties.
qs.ev: frankly I agree with them
qs.x: “Frankly I agree with them” shows she supports the rule, pointing to the risk of a personal policy running out after a serious accident. She never suggests suspending or relaxing it.

qs.q: Why is Tariq concerned about pausing the program?
o: Drivers might leave and be hard to replace.
Clients might switch to a competing service.
The hospital might cancel clients’ appointments.
The board might close the program for good.
qs.ev: I’m worried we’ll lose them if the program goes on hold, even briefly.
qs.x: Tariq fears losing drivers during even a brief pause, and Agnes adds that recruiting them took two years. Competing services and permanent closure are never mentioned.

lines: Okay, the broker came back. The cheapest commercial quote is ninety-six hundred dollars a year. That’s three times our budget.
Ouch. Could we raise it? A special appeal to donors?

We could try, but we already ran the winter appeal in December, and the spring gala money is committed to the kitchen renovation. I don’t want to go back to the same people with another emergency three months later.
Fair. What about giving clients taxi vouchers while we sort it out?

I priced it. The average ride is about twenty-eight dollars each way, and almost every trip is a round trip. Sixty rides a month at fifty-six dollars is over three thousand a month. We’d burn through the whole year’s transportation budget by summer.
And the city’s accessible transit service? Some of our clients must qualify.

A few do, and they should register regardless. But most of our people don’t have a disability that would make them eligible. They just don’t drive anymore, or they can’t after a treatment. And dialysis patients are exhausted afterwards; nobody should be taking two regular buses home.
The broker mentioned something I hadn’t heard of: a provincial insurance pool for non-profits. Member organizations share the risk, so premiums are lower. Our quote would be forty-one hundred.
That’s only nine hundred over budget. What’s the catch?
Every volunteer has to submit a driver’s abstract, that’s their official driving record, and complete a two-hour online safety course within sixty days of joining.
That’s not a catch. That’s good practice.

qs.q: Why does Agnes reject a special donor appeal?
o: The gala raised less money than expected.
The board does not allow emergency appeals.
Donors were already approached recently.
Donors would rather fund the kitchen project.
qs.ev: I don’t want to go back to the same people with another emergency three months later.
qs.x: The winter appeal ran in December, and she doesn’t want to ask the same donors again three months later. The gala money is committed to the kitchen; nothing says it fell short.

qs.q: What does Agnes conclude about taxi vouchers?
o: They would be cheaper than a commercial policy.
They would exhaust the yearly budget too fast.
Most clients would refuse to use them.
They would only cover one-way trips.
qs.ev: We’d burn through the whole year’s transportation budget by summer.
qs.x: At over $3,000 a month, vouchers would use up the year’s transportation budget by summer – far more than any insurance quote. She calculates round trips, so one-way trips are not the issue.

qs.q: Why can most clients not use the city’s accessible transit service?
o: The service does not go to the hospital.
They live outside the service area.
Its routes require two bus transfers.
They do not meet its eligibility rules.
qs.ev: most of our people don’t have a disability that would make them eligible
qs.x: Most clients don’t have a qualifying disability; they simply no longer drive. The two buses she mentions refer to regular transit after dialysis, not to accessible transit.

lines: Good news. I spoke to the pool administrator. They can accept us, but coverage only starts on the first of a month, and they need the application by the twentieth to start on the first.
Today’s the eighth. And our current coverage ends on the thirtieth, so if we make the twentieth, there’s no gap at all.
Exactly. The application itself is simple. The tricky part is the abstracts. Each volunteer has to order their own from the province, and it costs twelve dollars.
We should reimburse them. Asking retirees to pay so they can keep volunteering doesn’t sit right with me.
Agreed. That’s under two hundred dollars. What about the nine-hundred-dollar gap in the premium?
The Westside Service Club has a small grants program for seniors’ services. Their next deadline is the end of the month, and I know the treasurer. I’ll call her this afternoon.
Then I’ll take it from the contingency line and explain it to the board. Nine hundred dollars to keep thirty-eight people getting to treatment is not a hard argument to make.
I’ll email the volunteers tonight about the abstracts. Should I mention the course as well?
Mention it, but don’t make a big deal of it. They have sixty days. Lead with the abstracts, because that’s the part with a real deadline.

qs.q: Why is the twentieth an important date?
o: Applying by then avoids any gap in coverage.
It is the day the current policy expires.
It is the service club’s grant deadline.
Volunteers must finish the course by then.
qs.ev: they need the application by the twentieth to start on the first
qs.x: Applying by the 20th means pool coverage starts on the 1st, right after the current policy ends on the 30th – no gap. The grant deadline is the end of the month, and the course allows sixty days.

qs.q: How does Tariq plan to cover the premium shortfall if the grant is refused?
o: By asking each volunteer to pay a small fee
By delaying the start of the new policy
By drawing on reserves and telling the board
By reducing the number of rides offered
qs.ev: Then I’ll take it from the contingency line and explain it to the board.
qs.x: If the service club says no, he will use the contingency line and explain it to the board. Volunteers will actually be reimbursed for their abstracts, not charged a fee.

parts.context: A passenger who has missed a train connection is speaking with an agent at a railway station.

lines: Hi, I hope you can help. My train from Windsor got in an hour and forty minutes late, and I missed my connection to North Bay. It left at four ten.

I’m sorry about that. Let me pull up your booking. Okay, Yasmin Haddad, travelling with a bicycle. Since the delay was on our side, there’s no charge to rebook you. The next train to North Bay leaves at six forty this evening.
That’s fine. I can wait a couple of hours.
The problem is the bike. The six forty is one of our older trains, and it doesn’t have bike racks. Bikes only go on trains with a baggage car, and the next one of those is tomorrow at nine fifteen.
Tomorrow? I’m supposed to start a cycling tour on Saturday morning. I’d planned to arrive tonight and put everything together at the hotel.

There are a couple of options. You could stay overnight here and take the nine fifteen with your bike. We’d cover a hotel room, since you missed the connection because of us. Or you take the six forty tonight, and we ship the bike separately on tomorrow’s train. It would reach North Bay station around four in the afternoon.
Is there a charge for shipping it?
Normally twenty-five dollars, but I’ll waive it because of the delay. You’d need to box it, though. We sell bike boxes here for fifteen.

Hmm. If I go tonight, I’m without the bike until tomorrow afternoon, but I’d have the morning free to pick up groceries and check in with the tour group. And the tour doesn’t start until Saturday anyway.
That’s right. And honestly, the hotel we use near the station here isn’t the nicest. I’d probably choose the evening train myself.
Ha, that’s refreshingly honest. Okay, I’ll take the six forty and ship the bike. Can I also get something to eat? I haven’t had lunch.
Since the delay was more than an hour, you’re entitled to a fifteen-dollar meal voucher. The café upstairs accepts it. Just bring the bike back here once it’s boxed, and I’ll tag it.
Perfect. Thanks for making this so painless.

qs.q: Why can Yasmin not take her bicycle on the six forty train?
o: It is already fully booked.
Bikes must be shipped a day ahead.
It is not equipped to carry them.
Her ticket does not include baggage.
qs.ev: it doesn’t have bike racks
qs.x: The 6:40 is an older train without bike racks; bikes go only on trains with a baggage car. Nothing says the train is full, and shipping a day ahead is not a rule.

qs.q: Why does the railway offer to pay for a hotel?
o: The railway caused her to miss her train.
She is travelling with a bicycle.
The station closes overnight.
Her tour group requested it.
qs.ev: since you missed the connection because of us
qs.x: The hotel is offered because she missed the connection “because of us” – the railway’s delay. The bicycle only explains why she might need to stay over.

qs.q: Why does Yasmin decide to travel that evening?
o: The hotel near the station is fully booked.
She needs her bike for a ride that evening.
The bike shipping fee will be waived.
She wants a free morning to get ready.
qs.ev: I’d have the morning free to pick up groceries and check in with the tour group
qs.x: Arriving tonight gives her a free morning for groceries and meeting the tour group before Saturday. The waived fee is a bonus, not her reason, and the hotel is never said to be full.

qs.q: What does the agent imply about the hotel?
o: It is not of very good quality.
It is too far from the station.
It does not accept bicycles.
It must be paid for in advance.
qs.ev: the hotel we use near the station here isn’t the nicest
qs.x: “Isn’t the nicest” suggests the hotel is not very good, which is why he would choose the evening train. It is “near the station”, so distance isn’t the issue.

qs.q: What must Yasmin do before her bicycle can be tagged?
o: Pay the twenty-five-dollar fee
Pack it in a box
Show her meal voucher
Remove its front wheel
qs.ev: Just bring the bike back here once it’s boxed, and I’ll tag it.
qs.x: The agent will tag the bike “once it’s boxed”; boxes cost $15 at the station. The $25 shipping fee is waived because of the delay.

parts.context: A father calls a driving school to ask about a course for his daughter.

lines: Good afternoon, Northway Driving School, Ruth speaking.
Hi, Ruth. My name’s Emeka. My daughter just got her learner’s licence, and I’m trying to understand what your beginner course involves before I sign her up.
Of course. Our beginner course is approved by the province. It’s twenty hours of classroom instruction, ten hours of homework, and ten hours of driving in one of our cars with an instructor.

Seven ninety-five plus tax for the standard version, where the classroom part is in person over two weekends. There’s also an online version of the classroom part that students do at their own pace. That one’s seven forty-five.
Fifty dollars less. Is the online one any less thorough?
Same content, same exam at the end. Some students do better in a room with a teacher, though. The online version has to be finished within six months, and honestly, some teenagers let it drift.
Mine might, to be fair. What’s the actual benefit of the course? A friend said it lets them take the road test sooner.

That’s right. Normally a new driver has to wait twelve months before the first road test. With a certificate from an approved course, that drops to eight. And most insurance companies give a discount for the certificate, although we can’t tell you how much. That depends on the insurer.
Okay. When does the next in-person group start?
The one starting Saturday the fourth is full, I’m afraid. The next one begins on the eighteenth.
Hmm. She has swim meets most weekends in the spring, so two full weekends would be tough anyway. I think the online version might suit her better, as long as I keep an eye on her progress.
We send parents a weekly progress report, so that helps.
Good. And the driving lessons, where do they start?
The instructor picks her up at home or at school. Within city limits that’s included. If you’re outside the city, it’s twenty dollars extra per lesson.
We’re in town, so that’s fine. What if she has to cancel a lesson?
We need twenty-four hours’ notice; otherwise there’s a fifty-dollar charge. Illness with a doctor’s note is the exception.
Last question. For the road test itself, can she use your car? Ours is a bit, well, battered.

Yes, we have a road test package: a one-hour warm-up lesson just before the test, and use of the car for the test itself. That’s one sixty. Students who use it tend to be calmer, because they’re driving a car they already know.
That makes sense. I’ll talk to her tonight and call you back to register.

qs.q: What is the main difference between the two versions of the course?
o: Only the in-person version leads to a certificate.
The online one is self-paced and costs less.
The online version includes fewer driving hours.
The in-person version has a harder final exam.
qs.ev: There’s also an online version of the classroom part that students do at their own pace.
qs.x: The online classroom portion is done at the student’s own pace and costs $50 less. Ruth says the content and final exam are the same, and driving hours are not reduced.

qs.q: What concern does Ruth raise about the online version?
o: It is harder for students to pass the exam.
Insurers may not accept its certificate.
Parents cannot see how students are doing.
Some teenagers fail to finish it on time.
qs.ev: honestly, some teenagers let it drift
qs.x: It must be finished within six months, and some teens “let it drift”. Parents actually receive weekly progress reports, and the exam and certificate are the same.

qs.q: According to Ruth, what does the course certificate allow?
o: An earlier first road test
A guaranteed insurance discount
A shorter final exam
Free use of the school car
qs.ev: With a certificate from an approved course, that drops to eight.
qs.x: The certificate cuts the wait for the first road test from twelve to eight months. Insurance discounts depend on the insurer, so nothing is guaranteed.

qs.q: Why does Emeka choose the online version?
o: The in-person classes are full until summer.
It includes more in-car lessons.
His daughter’s weekends are often taken.
His daughter prefers learning on her own.
qs.ev: She has swim meets most weekends in the spring
qs.x: Swim meets on most spring weekends make two full in-person weekends difficult. Only the group on the fourth is full; another starts on the eighteenth.

qs.q: In which case would a late cancellation not be charged?
o: If the student lives outside city limits
If it is the student’s very first lesson
If a parent calls the instructor directly
If the student brings a doctor’s note
qs.ev: Illness with a doctor’s note is the exception.
qs.x: Cancelling with less than 24 hours’ notice costs $50, except for illness with a doctor’s note. Living outside the city affects pickup fees, not cancellations.

qs.q: Why does Ruth recommend the road test package?
o: They are calmer in a car they know.
The school’s cars are easier to drive.
Examiners prefer the school’s vehicles.
It is cheaper than a regular lesson.
qs.ev: Students who use it tend to be calmer, because they’re driving a car they already know.
qs.x: Students are calmer using a car they know from their lessons. Emeka’s battered car is his own worry; nothing is said about examiners preferring school cars.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a new fee at an airport.

lines: Travellers being dropped off at Lakehead International Airport will soon have to pay for the privilege. Starting March first, private vehicles stopping at the departures curb will be charged five dollars for up to ten minutes, with the fee collected automatically through licence-plate cameras and billed by mail or through a prepaid account. Vehicles that stay longer than ten minutes will pay an additional five dollars for every five minutes.
Airport spokesperson Tamsin Hale says the fee is less about revenue than about congestion.

During the morning peak, cars are backed up onto the access road, sometimes for a kilometre. People wait at the curb for fifteen, twenty minutes while their passenger checks a bag. Emergency vehicles have had trouble getting through. We need people to treat the curb as a drop-off zone, not a waiting room.

The airport is also offering an alternative. Drivers can use the economy parking lot, which is connected to the terminal by a free shuttle every eight minutes, and stop there for up to thirty minutes at no charge. Taxis, licensed ride-hailing vehicles and accessible transit vans are exempt from the curb fee, though ride-hailing companies have said they will pass on a fee of their own.

Several other Canadian airports have introduced similar fees, and at one of them, curbside waiting times fell by half within the first year. But critics, including a local seniors’ advocacy group, say the shuttle is not a realistic option for travellers with heavy luggage or limited mobility. The airport says drivers with a valid accessible parking permit will be able to register their plate in advance and be exempted from the fee. Registration will open online two weeks before the fee takes effect.

qs.q: How will the curb fee be collected?
o: By attendants standing at the curb
By cameras that identify each vehicle
At pay stations inside the terminal
By the airlines at check-in
qs.ev: the fee collected automatically through licence-plate cameras
qs.x: Licence-plate cameras identify vehicles, and the fee is billed by mail or through a prepaid account. No attendants, pay stations or airlines are involved.

qs.q: According to Tamsin Hale, what is the main purpose of the fee?
o: To raise money for a new terminal
To encourage travellers to take transit
To discourage ride-hailing at the airport
To keep cars from lingering at the curb
qs.ev: We need people to treat the curb as a drop-off zone, not a waiting room.
qs.x: She says the fee is “less about revenue than about congestion”: drivers waiting at the curb back traffic onto the access road. Transit and ride-hailing are not her stated aims.

qs.q: How much will a driver pay if they stop at the departures curb for 20 minutes?
qs.ev: Vehicles that stay longer than ten minutes will pay an additional five dollars for every five minutes.
qs.x: The first ten minutes cost $5; the next ten minutes are two five-minute periods at $5 each, so $5 + $10 = $15. $10 counts only one extra period.

qs.q: What can be inferred about ride-hailing passengers?
o: They must now use the economy lot instead.
They are banned from the departures curb.
They may still end up paying an extra fee.
They will get a discount on airport parking.
qs.ev: ride-hailing companies have said they will pass on a fee of their own
qs.x: Ride-hailing vehicles are exempt from the airport’s fee, but the companies plan to pass on their own fee, so riders may still pay. They are not banned from the curb.

qs.q: How has the airport responded to the seniors’ group?
o: By exempting drivers with accessible permits
By adding a second free shuttle route
By extending the free period to thirty minutes
By delaying the fee until the summer
qs.ev: drivers with a valid accessible parking permit will be able to register their plate in advance and be exempted from the fee
qs.x: Permit holders can pre-register their plate and avoid the fee. The thirty free minutes apply to the economy lot, not the curb, and no delay is announced.

parts.context: Three friends are planning a two-week road trip from Winnipeg to the Rocky Mountains.

lines: Okay, we’ve put this off long enough. If we’re leaving on the eighth of September, we need to decide how we’re actually doing this trip. I still think we should rent an RV.
Because it makes sense! Two weeks, Winnipeg to Jasper and back. With an RV, we sleep wherever we want, we cook our own meals, we never have to pack and unpack a tent in the rain.
I’ll admit the not-packing-a-tent part sounds good. My back hasn’t been the same since that canoe trip.

I actually looked it up last night. The cheapest RV I could find for fourteen days is thirty-eight hundred dollars. That includes fifteen hundred kilometres. After that, it’s thirty-five cents a kilometre.

About forty-five hundred kilometres with the side trips you wanted. So that’s three thousand extra kilometres, another ten fifty. Plus fuel. Those things use something like twenty-five litres per hundred kilometres, which is more than three times what Teodor’s car burns.
Okay, that’s more than I thought. I’d been looking at the daily rate and ignoring the kilometres.
So we’re talking well over six thousand dollars before we’ve bought a single meal. Split three ways, that’s two thousand each just for the vehicle.
Fine. I hear you. The RV is a lovely dream. What’s your plan, Kwame?
Teodor’s car, and we camp the whole way. Campsites are thirty or forty dollars a night, split three ways. It’s by far the cheapest.
Hang on. Nobody asked me if I want to put forty-five hundred kilometres on my car.
I assumed you’d be fine with it. It’s a good car.

It is a good car, and I’d like it to stay that way. I don’t mind driving it, but it’s not just gas. Tires, oil changes, wear and tear. If we’re using my car, I think it’s fair that we account for that.

That’s completely reasonable. What if we each chip in for gas and also pay Teodor something per kilometre? The government rate is way too high, but ten cents a kilometre would be about four hundred and fifty dollars.
That would make me feel a lot better, honestly.
Fine by me. So, car and camping.
Car, yes. Camping the whole way, I’m less sure. Mid-September in the Rockies, it can go below zero at night. I’ve done that once. I spent the whole night wearing every piece of clothing I owned.
What if we split it? Camp on the Prairies, where it’s still warm in September and the campsites are cheap, and then get cabins or a motel once we hit the mountains?
Not in town, no. But there are motels in Hinton, forty minutes away, for about a hundred and forty a night. Split three ways, that’s under fifty each.
Hmm. That’s still more than camping. But I suppose I’d rather not wake up to frost on my sleeping bag either.
So: my car, gas split three ways plus ten cents a kilometre to me, tents on the Prairies, a motel in Hinton for the mountain nights. I can live with that.
Deal. I’ll book the campsites tonight; some of the provincial parks fill up even in September.
And I’ll book Hinton. Four nights?
Make it five. If it rains, I’m not getting back in a tent.

qs.q: Why does Shauna initially prefer renting an RV?
o: It would be cheaper than camping.
It would offer flexibility and comfort.
Teodor’s car is too small for three people.
Campsites in Jasper are fully booked.
qs.ev: With an RV, we sleep wherever we want, we cook our own meals, we never have to pack and unpack a tent in the rain.
qs.x: She praises sleeping anywhere, cooking their own meals and never packing a wet tent – flexibility and comfort. She later admits she ignored the real cost, so price isn’t her reason.

qs.q: Why does Shauna give up on the RV idea?
o: The RV would not be allowed in most campsites.
Teodor refuses to drive such a large vehicle.
She realizes she overlooked the distance charges.
She learns that RVs cannot enter the national park.
qs.ev: I’d been looking at the daily rate and ignoring the kilometres.
qs.x: She admits she looked only at the daily rate and ignored the per-kilometre charges, which add $1,050. Teodor actually likes the idea of not packing a tent, and campsite rules are never mentioned.

qs.q: According to Teodor, roughly what would the RV cost before food?
o: More than six thousand dollars
About thirty-eight hundred dollars
Roughly two thousand dollars
Just over ten thousand dollars
qs.ev: So we’re talking well over six thousand dollars before we’ve bought a single meal.
qs.x: $3,800 rental + $1,050 for extra kilometres + fuel = well over $6,000. $3,800 is only the base rental, and about $2,000 is each person’s share.

qs.q: What is Teodor’s attitude when Kwame assumes they will use his car?
o: He is happy to lend it at no cost.
He refuses to let anyone else drive it.
He thinks it is too old for a long trip.
He is irritated that he was not consulted.
qs.ev: Nobody asked me if I want to put forty-five hundred kilometres on my car.
qs.x: “Hang on. Nobody asked me” shows annoyance at being taken for granted. He then agrees to drive if wear and tear is covered, so he doesn’t refuse, and he calls it a good car.

qs.q: What arrangement does Shauna propose for using Teodor’s car?
o: Teodor covers gas while the others pay for sites
They share fuel and pay him a set rate per kilometre
They reimburse him at the government mileage rate
They pay for any repairs needed after the trip
qs.ev: ten cents a kilometre would be about four hundred and fifty dollars
qs.x: Shauna suggests sharing gas and paying Teodor ten cents a kilometre, about $450. She says the government rate is “way too high”, so they won’t use it.

qs.q: Why is Teodor reluctant to camp for the whole trip?
o: He has suffered through very cold nights before.
He thinks the campsites will all be fully booked.
He prefers to stay in Jasper’s town centre.
He dislikes cooking meals outdoors.
qs.ev: I spent the whole night wearing every piece of clothing I owned.
qs.x: He warns that Rockies nights go below zero and recalls a night spent wearing all his clothes. Shauna, not Teodor, mentions campsites filling up, and staying in Jasper’s centre is never proposed.

qs.q: How does Kwame respond to the motel plan?
o: He rejects it because it costs too much.
He prefers cabins in Jasper instead.
He accepts it with some hesitation.
He suggests camping in the mountains anyway.
qs.ev: That’s still more than camping. But I suppose I’d rather not wake up to frost on my sleeping bag either.
qs.x: He notes it costs more than camping, but “I suppose I’d rather not wake up to frost” – hesitant acceptance. He is the one who said Jasper cabins aren’t cheap.

qs.q: What does the group finally decide about the mountain part of the trip?
o: Camp for four nights near Jasper
Rent a cabin in Jasper for five nights
Stay in Hinton only if it rains
Spend five nights in a Hinton motel
qs.ev: Make it five. If it rains, I’m not getting back in a tent.
qs.x: Kwame offers to book Hinton for four nights, but Teodor says “Make it five”. Rain is his reason for the extra night, not a condition for staying there at all.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about a proposed charge for driving downtown.

lines: For years, the idea of charging drivers to enter the downtown core has been raised in city halls across Canada, and just as quickly dropped. Now our city’s transportation committee has asked staff to study a congestion charge for real, and the early reaction suggests the debate will be anything but simple.

The proposal on the table would charge private vehicles twelve dollars to enter the core on weekdays between seven a.m. and seven p.m. City staff estimate it would reduce traffic downtown by about eighteen percent and raise roughly ninety million dollars a year, which would be set aside for transit. Supporters, including the regional board of trade, argue that congestion already acts as a tax, one paid in lost time. A delivery driver stuck in gridlock for an hour costs a business money whether or not anyone sends a bill. Better, they say, to charge directly and use the money to give people alternatives.

Downtown merchants are less enthusiastic. The Downtown Business Association warns that shoppers who can easily drive to a suburban mall with free parking may simply stop coming. Its chair points to a pharmacy owner who estimates that a third of her customers arrive by car. She doesn’t object to the principle, the chair says, but she can’t afford to be the experiment.

Equity is another sticking point. Critics argue that a flat charge falls hardest on lower-income workers who drive because transit doesn’t serve their shifts or neighbourhoods, while wealthier commuters will barely notice the fee. Supporters respond that, according to the city’s own travel survey, the people who drive into the core at rush hour have, on average, higher incomes than those who take transit, so the charge would, if anything, shift money from wealthier to less wealthy residents.

Transportation economist Dr. Anika Varga, who has studied charges in several European cities, says the record is encouraging but comes with a warning. In nearly every case, she says, the charge was unpopular before it began and gained support once residents saw quieter streets and faster buses. The key, in her view, is sequencing: transit improvements have to arrive before the charge does, or at the very least at the same time. Charging people before giving them a real alternative, she says, is the surest way to kill the idea.

Staff are expected to report back in the fall. Councillors on the committee have signalled that they will not support any charge without discounts for low-income residents and an exemption for people with disabilities, and several have said privately that a vote is unlikely before the next municipal election.

qs.q: What argument does the board of trade make?
o: Drivers already pay a hidden cost in lost time.
Most delivery drivers support the charge.
The charge should apply only on weekends.
Downtown businesses would earn more parking revenue.
qs.ev: congestion already acts as a tax, one paid in lost time
qs.x: The board of trade says congestion is already a tax paid in lost time, so charging directly is better. The delivery driver is an example of that cost, not evidence that drivers support the charge.

qs.q: What is the pharmacy owner’s position?

p1.meta: From: Margit Sandvik  |  To: Anders Sandvik  |  Subject: A proposal about the wagon
p1.text:
Dear Anders,

I hope the move into the new office went smoothly and that Freya is getting excited about September. I have a proposal for you, and I want you to feel completely free to say no.

As you know, I moved downtown in March, mainly to be closer to work. What I didn’t expect was how quickly I would stop needing the car. The office is a twelve-minute walk, the grocery store is downstairs, and for the rare trip to the hardware store, I use one of the car-share vehicles parked around the corner. I checked this morning: I haven’t driven the wagon in six weeks. Meanwhile, I’m paying two hundred and ten dollars a month for a parking spot in my building, plus insurance, for a car that mostly collects dust.

So here is my idea. Would Freya like it for university? I know Lethbridge has decent buses, but you mentioned she’ll be doing placements at rural schools in her second year, and those are hard to reach without a car. I would sell it to you for one dollar, purely to make the paperwork simple. You would only need to cover the transfer fees and registration.

Before you decide, I should be honest about its condition. It’s eight years old and runs beautifully, but at the last oil change, the mechanic told me the rear brakes will need replacing within the next five thousand kilometres. It would be fairer to get that done before Freya drives it, and I’m happy to pay for it.

I do have one small request. Every August, as you know, I spend a week at the lake with the Brunellis, and the bus out there runs only twice a week. Would it be possible to borrow the wagon back for that week? I would of course fill the tank.

I’ll admit it feels a little strange to let it go. That car has carried me through two moves and a great many road trips. But it would be lovely to know it’s still in the family.

Love,
Margit

p3.title: Designing Transit for Everyone
paras: When most people think of accessible transit, they picture a wheelchair ramp. Ramps matter, but accessibility experts argue that riders’ needs are far broader. Around one in five Canadians has a disability, and many of those disabilities are invisible: chronic pain, hearing loss, anxiety, or conditions that affect memory and concentration. Add older adults, parents pushing strollers, travellers with heavy luggage and people recovering from injuries, and the group that benefits from accessible design becomes something close to a majority of riders at one point or another. For that reason, planners increasingly talk about “universal design”: building systems that work for as many people as possible from the start, rather than adding special features later.

Some of the most effective changes are surprisingly simple. Automated stop announcements, both spoken and displayed on screens, help riders who are blind or deaf, but surveys show they are also appreciated by tourists, newcomers and anyone riding an unfamiliar route at night. Low-floor buses that kneel at the curb remove the need for a lift in most cases and speed up boarding for everyone, which helps buses stay on schedule. Even seating layout makes a difference: priority seats near the front, with enough space to turn a mobility device, reduce the awkward shuffle that can delay departures. Agencies that have introduced these features report fewer complaints overall, not only from riders with disabilities.

Stations present bigger challenges. Many older subway and commuter rail stations were built long before accessibility laws existed, and retrofitting them with elevators can cost tens of millions of dollars per station. Even where elevators exist, they are often out of service, and a single broken elevator can make an entire station unusable for a wheelchair user, who may have to travel several stops further and backtrack. Advocates argue that reliable maintenance deserves as much attention as new construction. Some agencies now publish real-time elevator status online, allowing riders to plan around outages, although critics note that a website is of little use to someone who discovers the problem only after arriving on the platform.

Technology is opening new possibilities, but it can also create barriers. Fare payment apps and touchscreen ticket machines can be difficult for people with low vision, limited dexterity or no smartphone, and several agencies have faced complaints after removing cash options. On the other hand, apps that provide step-by-step audio navigation through stations have been welcomed by many blind riders. Experts say the lesson is not to avoid technology but to involve disabled riders from the beginning of the design process. When agencies consult only after a product is finished, they often end up paying to fix problems that could have been prevented at little cost.

qs.x: Paragraph A: many disabilities are invisible, such as chronic pain or hearing loss.

p4.title: A Lower Number on a Sign Won’t Slow Our Streets
p4.byline: Opinion | by Garrett Lindahl, retired traffic engineer
p4.text:
Next month, council will vote on a proposal to lower the default speed limit on every residential street in the city from 50 km/h to 30 km/h. The motivation is admirable. A pedestrian struck at 30 km/h is far more likely to survive than one struck at 50, and the physics of that are not up for debate. If I believed that changing a number on a sign would change the speed at which people drive, I would support the motion without hesitation. After thirty-four years as a traffic engineer, I do not.

Here is the uncomfortable truth my profession learned long ago: drivers choose their speed mostly according to how a street looks and feels, not according to the sign. A wide, straight road with good sightlines and no parked cars invites speed, whatever the posted limit says. When cities lower limits without changing the street, average speeds typically fall by only two or three kilometres an hour. That is not nothing, but it is a long way from thirty.

The gap between the posted limit and actual behaviour creates its own problems. When most drivers on a street are breaking the law, enforcement becomes arbitrary. Police cannot ticket everyone, so they ticket some, and drivers come to see the limit as a revenue tool rather than a safety measure. Meanwhile, pedestrians and parents may assume that a 30 sign means traffic is moving at 30, and let their guard down accordingly.

None of this means we should accept the status quo. Streets where children walk to school, streets bordering parks and narrow streets with no sidewalks should absolutely have lower limits. But those lower limits must come with physical changes that make 30 feel natural: curb extensions that narrow the road at intersections, raised crosswalks, speed humps, planters and on-street parking that breaks up long, straight stretches. Several neighbourhoods in our own city have done exactly this, and measured speeds there have dropped by ten kilometres an hour or more.

Supporters of the city-wide motion will say that it is a first step, and that physical changes can follow. I would be more persuaded if the budget said so. The proposal sets aside two million dollars, almost all of it for new signs, and nothing at all for redesign. Signs are cheap; concrete is not. Once the signs are up and council has claimed a victory, I fear there will be little appetite for the more expensive work that actually slows cars down.

There is also a fairness issue that deserves more attention than it has received. Some residential streets in the city function as collector roads, carrying buses and thousands of vehicles a day. Dropping them to 30 would slow transit, and riders, many of whom have no car, would pay for it in longer trips.

My proposal is modest. Instead of a blanket change, council should identify the two hundred residential streets with the highest number of pedestrians and the worst collision records, lower the limit on those, and pair every new sign with physical measures within the same budget year. It would cover fewer streets at first. It would also work.

t2.intro: Your provincial government is planning a major transportation investment between two large cities that are 300 kilometres apart, and it is asking residents for their opinion.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer?
t2.a: Build a high-speed passenger rail line that would cut travel time between the two cities to 90 minutes. It would open in about 12 years.
t2.b: Widen the existing highway from four lanes to six to reduce congestion. The work would be finished in about 4 years.
t2.model:
Although the high-speed rail line is the more exciting idea, I would choose Option B, widening the highway, because it would solve a real problem much sooner and help more people.

The most important factor for me is timing. Twelve years is a very long wait, and large rail projects in Canada have a history of running late and over budget. The highway could be finished in four years. In the meantime, thousands of commuters, truck drivers and families would continue to lose hours in traffic every week.

Secondly, the highway serves everyone along the corridor, not just people travelling between the two big cities. Small towns in between depend on it for deliveries, tourism and access to hospitals, and a rail line with few stops would do little for them. Most freight also travels by truck, so a wider highway supports the regional economy directly.

I recognize that rail is cleaner, and that new lanes can eventually fill up with more traffic. However, as electric vehicles become more common, that environmental gap is narrowing. For these reasons, I believe Option B is the more practical investment.

t1.prompt: Your friend is moving from a small town to a large city for a new job. She owns a car and is not sure whether to bring it with her or sell it. Advise her.
t1.model: That’s a big move, congratulations! My honest advice would be to sell the car, or at least not to rush into bringing it, and let me explain why. In a big city, owning a car is a lot more expensive than in a small town. Insurance rates are usually much higher, and parking can be a nightmare. Many apartment buildings charge a hundred and fifty or two hundred dollars a month just for a spot, and parking downtown during the day can cost twenty dollars or more. On top of that, you’ll probably spend a lot of time sitting in traffic. Before you decide, look at where your new office is and where you’re planning to live. If you can get to work by subway or bus in under forty-five minutes, you probably won’t miss the car much. For weekend trips or big shopping runs, you can use a car-share service or rent a car now and then, and it’ll still cost far less than owning one. That said, if your job requires you to visit clients outside the city, or the transit near your new place is poor, it might be worth keeping. Maybe try living there for a couple of months first, and leave the car with your parents in the meantime.

t2.prompt: Talk about a memorable journey you took by train, bus or boat. Where were you going, and what made it memorable?
t2.model: One journey I’ll never forget was an overnight ferry I took with my family from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland when I was about twelve. We’d booked a tiny cabin with four bunk beds, and my brother and I argued over the top bunks for about an hour. What made it memorable, though, was the evening. My dad woke us up around ten and took us out on the deck, and the sky was completely clear. I had never seen so many stars in my life, because we’d always lived in the city. Then a crew member pointed out some dolphins following the boat, and we could see them jumping in the light from the windows. I barely slept that night because I was so excited. Even now, whenever I see the ocean, I think about that trip.

scene.alt: A snowy residential street on a winter morning, with snow still falling. Two houses stand in the background, one red and one beige, with pine trees beside them. In the middle of the street, a green car is stuck in a snowbank, and two people in winter hats are pushing it from behind. Nearby, a man in a blue jacket is shovelling snow from his driveway. On the right, a big yellow snowplow truck with “PLOW” written on it is coming down the street. On the left, a child in a purple jacket waves next to a snowman. An older man holding a cup stands on the right beside a black dog, watching.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This is a snowy residential street on a winter morning, and it’s still snowing quite a bit. In the background there are two houses, a red one and a beige one, with pine trees beside them. In the middle of the street, a green car seems to be stuck in a snowbank, and two people in winter hats are leaning in and pushing it from behind, trying to get it moving. Right next to them, a man in a blue jacket is shovelling snow off his driveway. On the right, a big yellow snowplow with the word Plow on the side is coming down the street. On the left, a little kid in a purple jacket is waving, standing beside a snowman. And on the right, an older man with a cup of coffee is standing next to a black dog, just watching everything.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think a few things will happen in the next few minutes. First, the two people pushing the green car will probably manage to get it free, but the wheels will likely spin and spray slush all over them, so they’ll end up laughing and covered in snow. Then the snowplow will come down the street, and unfortunately, it will probably push a big ridge of heavy snow right across the end of the driveway that the man in the blue jacket has just finished shovelling. He’ll most likely throw his hands up in frustration and have to start all over again. The older man with the coffee might offer to help, or at least sympathize. Meanwhile, the black dog will probably get excited by the noise of the plow and start barking, and the child by the snowman may run inside to stay out of the way.

t5.intro: You and your partner have a 6:00 a.m. flight and need to be at the airport by 4:00 a.m. You are deciding how to get there. Choose the option you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade your partner that your choice is better than the one they prefer.

options.title: Taxi
details: Picks you up at your door at 3:20 a.m.
Must be booked the night before

options.title: Airport express bus
details: First bus leaves downtown at 3:30 a.m.
Stop is a 10-minute walk from home

other.title: Driving and parking at the airport
details: $24 per day in the long-term lot
Shuttle from lot to terminal every 15 minutes
Car is waiting when you return

t5.persuade: Your partner prefers driving and parking at the airport. Persuade your partner that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know driving ourselves feels like the most independent option, but I really think the taxi makes more sense for this trip. First, think about the timing. If we drive, we leave at three-thirty, park in the long-term lot, then wait for a shuttle that only comes every fifteen minutes. If we just miss one, we’re cutting it close for a six o’clock flight. The taxi picks us up at our door and drops us right at departures. Second, the cost is closer than it looks. Parking for four days is ninety-six dollars, plus gas. The taxi is sixty-five each way, so yes, it’s a bit more, but not by much. And honestly, after a long flight home, the last thing I want is to drive at midnight when I’m exhausted. Let’s book the taxi tonight and actually relax on the way.

t6.situation: You lent your car to a close friend for the weekend. When you got it back, you noticed a new dent and a long scratch on the rear bumper, but your friend did not mention them. The repair will cost about $700. Your spouse wants you to make an insurance claim, but you would lose your claims-free discount.
options: Talk to your friend and ask about the damage.
Talk to your spouse and explain why you do not want to make an insurance claim.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey Jordan, thanks again for bringing the car back on Sunday, and I hope the trip to the cottage was fun. I wanted to ask you about something, and I hope it doesn’t come across the wrong way. When I washed the car yesterday, I noticed a dent and a long scratch on the rear bumper that weren’t there before. I’m not accusing you of anything; maybe it happened in a parking lot and you didn’t even notice. But I wanted to talk to you directly rather than wonder about it. The body shop quoted me about seven hundred dollars, and if I go through insurance, I’ll lose my claims-free discount, which would cost me even more. Would you be willing to split the repair with me? Honestly, our friendship matters much more to me than a bumper, so I’d really like us to sort this out together.

t7.prompt: Answer the following question: Should the minimum age for getting a driver’s licence be raised to 18? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: In my opinion, the minimum age shouldn’t be raised to eighteen, although I do think the rules for young drivers could be stricter. My first reason is that, in much of Canada, a licence isn’t a luxury. In rural areas and small towns, there’s often no bus at all, and a sixteen-year-old may need to drive to school, to a part-time job or to help a family member get to appointments. Raising the age would put a real burden on those families. Secondly, I believe experience matters more than age. Research suggests that new drivers are most at risk in their first year behind the wheel, whatever their age. An eighteen-year-old with no experience isn’t automatically safer than a seventeen-year-old who has spent a year driving with a parent beside them. That’s why graduated licensing makes sense: young drivers start with restrictions, like zero alcohol and limits on night driving and passengers, and they earn more freedom gradually. If we want to improve safety, I’d rather see more required practice hours and stricter enforcement of those restrictions. So, overall, I think we should keep the age at sixteen but make the learning period more demanding.

scene.alt: On a city sidewalk stands an enormous yellow dog sculpture, sitting with its tail raised; it is about as tall as a two-storey building. A speech bubble beside its head reads “NEXT BUS: 4 MIN”, as if it were a digital sign. To the right are an ordinary “BUS STOP” sign and a bench, where a woman sits looking at her phone. A child beside her points up at the giant dog, and a man in a grey coat stands nearby. Behind them is a grey office building labelled “TRANSIT”, and a streetlamp stands on the left.

t8.prompt: Your city is choosing a design for new bus shelters, and you have seen this unusual proposal. Call a friend who works for the city, describe the design, and explain whether you think the city should choose it. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hi Ahmed, it’s me. I just saw the designs for the new bus shelters on the city website, and one of them is, well, unusual. Picture a giant yellow dog, about as tall as a two-storey building, sitting on the sidewalk right beside the bus stop with its tail in the air. Next to its head there’s a speech bubble that’s actually a digital screen, and it tells you when the next bus is coming, like “Next bus: four minutes”. There’s an ordinary bench and a bus stop sign beside it. Honestly, I love it as public art, and kids would adore it. But I don’t think the city should choose it for a bus stop. It doesn’t give anyone shelter from rain or snow, and in January that’s what riders need most. Maybe the dog could go in a park instead, with a practical shelter at the stop.
